stages.title: Budgeting & Cash Flow
stages.description: How to compare what comes in with what goes out, separate needs from wants, track spending and use a simple framework such as 50/30/20 to plan a monthly budget.
learningObjectives: Explain a budget as a plan comparing income with expenses, and what a surplus or deficit means
Distinguish needs from wants with everyday examples
Describe practical ways to track spending before setting a budget
Apply the 50/30/20 split to a monthly take-home (net) income as one example method

explainBack.question: A friend just got their first job and keeps running out of money before month-end. Explain how they could build a simple monthly budget, including how to track spending, how to sort needs from wants, and how the 50/30/20 rule would split their take-home pay.
rubric: A budget compares income with expenses: a positive difference is a surplus that can go to savings or paying debt; a negative one means cutting spending or raising income
Needs are essentials (e.g. housing, food, utilities, transport, insurance); wants are non-essential (e.g. dining out, entertainment, brand-name extras)
Track actual spending first (receipts, a journal or app, by category, starting with a week at a time) before setting limits
The 50/30/20 rule puts about 50% of monthly net (take-home) income toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward savings; it is a guideline, not a fixed law
Saving = income minus expenditure; 'paying yourself first' means setting savings aside before spending on wants

resources.title: The 50-30-20 Rule - Budgeting for Needs, Wants, and Savings
resources.description: A short explainer on splitting income into needs, wants and savings using the 50/30/20 guideline.
keyPoints: Introduces the 50/30/20 budgeting guideline
Explains the difference between needs and wants
Shows how a savings share fits into a monthly plan

resources.title: Budgeting: How to create a budget and stick with it
resources.description: A US regulator's step-by-step guide to listing income, tracking spending, mapping bill dates and building a working budget.
keyPoints: Step 1: list every source of income
Step 2: track spending by category, starting with one week at a time
Step 3: map bill due dates against when income arrives to avoid missed payments
Step 4: combine everything into a monthly budget worksheet and set a savings goal

resources.title: Financial Literacy Booklet (Financial Education Handbook)
resources.description: India's national financial-education body explains needs vs wants, income and expenses, budgeting, saving and other basics in plain language.
keyPoints: Defines a need as essential and a want as a non-essential desire
A budget compares income with expenses; surplus can repay debt or raise savings
Suggests recording daily expenses and totalling them over about three months
Saving = income - expenditure; pay yourself first
Advises clearing high-interest debt before building savings

resources.title: 50/30/20 Budget (FE222h)
resources.description: A one-page university extension worksheet that applies the 50/30/20 split to monthly net income.
keyPoints: 50% of monthly net income for needs, 30% for wants, 20% for savings
Needs include groceries, housing, utilities, insurance and loan payments
Wants include dining out, entertainment and brand-name clothing
Unused 'wants' money can be moved to savings

resources.title: How to Make a Budget
resources.author: Susan Collins-Smith
resources.description: A four-step extension guide: record net income, list fixed and flexible expenses, plan for periodic costs, then compare the totals.
keyPoints: Start from monthly net income (after taxes and deductions)
Separate fixed expenses (rent, loan EMIs) from flexible ones (food, clothing)
Divide yearly costs by 12 to set aside for them monthly
Track spending for at least a week; longer tracking gives a more accurate budget

stages.title: Emergency Fund & Banking Basics
stages.description: Why an emergency fund comes first, how big it is commonly suggested to be, where to keep it, and how deposit insurance (DICGC in India) protects bank deposits.
learningObjectives: Explain what an emergency fund is and why it helps avoid high-cost borrowing
State the common guideline of three to six months of essential expenses and how to build towards it
Describe where to keep an emergency fund: safe, separate and easy to access
Explain DICGC deposit insurance: what is covered and the ₹5 lakh limit

explainBack.question: Explain to a new earner what an emergency fund is, how much is commonly suggested, where it should be kept and how to start one. Then explain how much of their bank deposits is protected if an Indian bank fails.
rubric: An emergency fund is money set aside for unexpected costs (job loss, medical bills, urgent repairs) so you don't have to borrow or break long-term investments
Common guidance is three to six months of basic living expenses; starting with a small first target and automatic transfers is recommended
Keep it safe, separate from everyday spending money and easily accessible, e.g. an insured savings account
In India, DICGC insures deposits (savings, fixed, recurring) up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, covering principal plus interest together
Depositors pay nothing for DICGC cover; the bank pays the premium

resources.title: Emergency Funds: How Much To Save & How To Get Started
resources.description: A short explainer on sizing an emergency fund and practical first steps to build one.
keyPoints: Why emergency savings matter
How to decide how much to save
Practical steps to start and grow the fund

resources.title: Building an Emergency Savings Fund
resources.provider: Washington State Department of Financial Institutions
resources.description: A state regulator's guide on what an emergency fund is, how much to aim for, where to hold it and how to build it gradually.
keyPoints: An emergency fund is money saved for unexpected costs
Common advice: three to six months of basic living costs
Start with a small first goal, then keep adding
Keep it safe, separate and accessible, e.g. an insured savings account
Automatic transfers from each paycheck make it easier

resources.title: Bank Failure? DICGC to the rescue | Mint Primer
resources.description: A short explainer from Mint on how DICGC deposit insurance protects depositors when an Indian bank fails.
keyPoints: Explains what DICGC is
Describes how deposit insurance works if a bank fails
Covers the insured limit for depositors

resources.title: DICGC Information Booklet
resources.provider: Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC)
resources.description: The official booklet on which banks and deposits are insured, the coverage limit and how claims are paid.
keyPoints: Covers commercial, small finance, payments, regional rural and cooperative banks registered with DICGC
Savings, fixed and recurring deposits are insured
Limit: ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, principal and interest combined
Depositors pay no premium; banks pay it
Some deposits, e.g. from governments or other banks, are not covered

stages.title: Debt, Credit Cards & Credit Scores
stages.description: How credit card interest and minimum payments work, what a CIBIL credit score measures, and how to spot unauthorised digital lending apps.
learningObjectives: Explain how credit card interest is charged and how paying in full avoids it
Explain why paying only the minimum due is costly
Describe what a CIBIL score is, its range and the main factors that affect it
Recognise the warning signs of unauthorised digital lending apps and how to verify a lender

explainBack.question: A college friend has a new credit card and is getting loan offers from apps. Explain how card interest and minimum payments work, what a credit score is and what affects it, and what they should check before borrowing through an app.
rubric: Paying the full statement balance by the due date avoids interest on purchases during the grace (interest-free) period; carried balances are charged interest, typically calculated daily
Paying only the minimum leaves a balance on which interest keeps being added, so repayment can take years and cost much more overall
A CIBIL score is a three-digit summary of credit history ranging from 300 to 900; higher scores make loan approval easier
Key score factors: on-time payment history, credit utilisation (keeping balances low), credit mix and the number of recent credit enquiries

RBI advises borrowing only from banks, RBI-regulated NBFCs or state-regulated lenders, verifying the lender, never sharing KYC documents with unverified apps, and reporting unauthorised apps (e.g. on the Sachet portal)

resources.title: Minimum Payments on Credit Cards - Personal Finance Tips
resources.description: A US Federal Trade Commission short showing how paying only the minimum makes a small purchase cost far more over time.
keyPoints: Example: a $300 purchase paid at the minimum each month
Shows interest being added to the balance monthly
Total paid ends up well above the original price

resources.title: Understanding minimum payments
resources.description: A short CFPB learning guide on what a minimum payment is and what happens when you pay only that amount.
keyPoints: A minimum payment is the smallest amount due each month
Interest is added to what you owe each month
Paying only the minimum can take years, even decades, on high balances
Paying more, or the full amount, lowers total interest

resources.title: How does my credit card company calculate the amount of interest I owe?
resources.description: Explains daily interest calculation, APRs and how the grace period lets you avoid interest by paying in full.
keyPoints: Interest is usually computed daily on the average daily balance
Different balance types (purchases, cash advances) can have different rates
A grace period applies to new purchases if you don't carry a balance
Paying the full balance by the due date avoids purchase interest

resources.title: Know The Four Factors That Influence Your CIBIL Score | TransUnion CIBIL
resources.description: TransUnion CIBIL's own short on the four main factors behind a CIBIL score.
keyPoints: Covers the four main score factors
Explains why repayment behaviour matters
Links everyday credit habits to the score

resources.title: All You Need To Know About Your CIBIL Score And How It Is Calculated
resources.description: The bureau's explainer on the 300–900 score range and the factors that raise or lower it.
keyPoints: Score ranges from 300 to 900; above 750 is considered strong
Payment history: late payments and defaults hurt the score
High credit utilisation signals rising debt and can lower the score
Balanced credit mix helps; many recent enquiries can hurt
Check your report regularly and dispute errors

resources.title: RBI cautions against Unauthorised Digital Lending Platforms/Mobile Apps
resources.description: RBI's public warning about unauthorised loan apps, with steps to verify lenders and report problems.
keyPoints: Unauthorised apps charge excessive interest and hidden fees
They use harsh recovery methods and misuse phone data
Legitimate lenders: banks, RBI-registered NBFCs, state-regulated lenders
Never share KYC documents with unverified apps
Report unauthorised apps on the Sachet portal or to police

stages.title: Inflation, Compounding & Time Value of Money
stages.description: Why money today is worth more than money later, how inflation erodes purchasing power, how to get real return from nominal return, and how compounding and the Rule of 72 work.
learningObjectives: Define inflation and explain how it reduces purchasing power
Calculate an approximate real return from a nominal return and inflation
Explain compound vs simple interest and why starting early matters
Use the Rule of 72 to estimate doubling time

explainBack.question: Your fixed deposit pays 6% a year and inflation is 4%. Explain what inflation does to your money, what your real return is, how compounding differs from simple interest, and roughly how long money takes to double at 9% a year.
rubric: Inflation is the rate at which prices rise over a period (commonly a year, measured by a consumer price index); it reduces what a fixed amount of money can buy
Real return ≈ nominal return − inflation: 6% − 4% ≈ 2% real; if inflation exceeds the interest rate, purchasing power falls
Compound interest earns interest on previously earned interest, while simple interest is paid only on the original principal, so compounding grows faster over time
Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ annual rate, so about 8 years at 9%
Time value of money: money available now is worth more than the same amount later because it can earn returns; starting early gives compounding more time

resources.title: Introduction to inflation | Inflation - measuring the cost of living | Macroeconomics | Khan Academy
resources.description: Khan Academy's introduction to what inflation is and how price-level changes are measured.
keyPoints: Defines inflation as a general rise in prices
Introduces measuring prices with a basket of goods
Shows how inflation changes what money can buy

resources.title: Nominal interest, real interest, and inflation calculations | AP Macroeconomics | Khan Academy
resources.description: Works through the relationship between nominal interest, real interest and inflation with calculations.
keyPoints: Defines nominal and real interest rates
Shows real rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation
Works through numeric examples

resources.title: Investor.gov: Knowledge Worth Celebrating (Compound Interest)
resources.description: A short SEC Investor.gov piece on how compound interest grows savings over time.
keyPoints: Explains compound interest in simple terms
Shows the benefit of time and regular saving
Points to free Investor.gov calculators

resources.title: Inflation: Prices on the Rise
resources.author: Ceyda Oner
resources.description: An IMF back-to-basics article defining inflation, how the CPI measures it and who it hurts.
keyPoints: Inflation is the rate of increase in prices over a period, usually a year
CPI tracks price changes for a fixed basket of goods and services
If income rises slower than prices, real income and purchasing power fall
Savers on fixed rates lose when inflation exceeds their interest rate

resources.title: Financial Awareness Messages (FAME)
resources.description: RBI's financial-awareness booklet covering time value of money, inflation and real return, compounding, risk and digital safety.
keyPoints: Money now is worth more than the same amount later because it can earn
Example: 6% deposit with 4% inflation gives about 2% real return
Banks compound interest: ₹10,000 at 10% compounded quarterly for 10 years ≈ ₹26,851
Higher expected return comes with higher risk; diversify
Never share PIN, password or OTP; report fraud quickly

resources.title: What is compound interest?
resources.description: Explains compound vs simple interest with a worked example, the Rule of 72 and why starting early helps.
keyPoints: Compound interest is interest earned on interest
$100 at 5%: $105 after year 1, $110.25 after year 2, over $162 after 10 years
Rule of 72: divide 72 by the rate to estimate doubling time (9% ≈ 8 years)
Starting young gives compounding more time to work

stages.title: Investing Basics: Risk, Diversification & Mutual Funds
stages.description: The risk-return trade-off, main asset classes, diversification, how mutual funds, SIPs and index funds work, why costs matter, and the KYC requirement.
learningObjectives: Explain the relationship between risk and return and name the main asset classes
Explain diversification and how mutual funds provide it
Describe how a SIP works and what rupee cost averaging means
Explain what an index fund and an expense ratio are and why costs matter over time
State that KYC is required before investing in Indian securities markets

explainBack.question: A friend wants to start investing ₹2,000 a month. Explain the trade-off between risk and return, why diversification matters, how a SIP in a mutual fund works, and what an index fund and expense ratio are. (General education only, not advice on any product.)
rubric: Higher potential returns usually come with higher risk; equity is higher-risk/growth-oriented while debt is lower-risk/fixed income

Diversification ('don't put all your eggs in one basket') spreads money across and within asset classes to reduce the impact of any one investment; a mutual fund pools many investors' money into a diversified portfolio
A SIP invests a fixed amount at regular intervals; the same amount buys more units when prices are low and fewer when high (rupee cost averaging), which does not guarantee profit
An index fund passively tracks a market index; an expense ratio is the yearly percentage of fund assets used to pay operating costs, and higher fees compound into a noticeably smaller final value
KYC (identity and address verification, e.g. PAN/Aadhaar) is mandatory before investing in securities markets/mutual funds in India

resources.title: How do I invest? | Investments and retirement | Financial Literacy | Khan Academy
resources.description: Khan Academy's beginner overview of getting started with investing.
keyPoints: Overview of how individuals begin investing
Introduces investment accounts and funds
Frames investing as long-term

resources.title: Financial Education Booklet
resources.provider: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
resources.description: SEBI's financial education booklet on risk and return, asset classes, mutual funds, SIPs, KYC, frauds and grievance redressal.
keyPoints: Risk and investing go hand in hand; higher returns mean more uncertainty
Equity schemes are higher risk, debt schemes lower, hybrid in between
Don't put all eggs in one basket: diversify
SIPs invest a fixed amount regularly, from as little as ₹500 a month
KYC with PAN, Aadhaar or other ID and address proof is mandatory

resources.title: What is Rupee Cost Averaging?
resources.description: The mutual fund industry body's explanation of how regular SIP investing averages out purchase cost.
keyPoints: Regular SIPs buy more units when markets fall and fewer when they rise
Over long periods this can lower the average cost per unit
Removes the need to time market highs and lows
Works best with discipline over longer periods

resources.title: Index Funds
resources.description: Explains what index funds are, passive management, potential cost advantages and risks such as tracking error.
keyPoints: Index funds aim to track the return of a market index
They use a passive strategy with infrequent trading
Often cheaper, but not all index funds cost less than active funds
Risks include tracking error and inability to avoid market falls

resources.title: Expense Ratio
resources.description: Glossary definition of a fund's expense ratio and where to find it.
keyPoints: Expense ratio = share of a fund's average net assets used yearly for operating expenses
Includes management and other fees
Found in the fund's fee table (offer document)
Directly reduces investors' returns

resources.title: How Fees and Expenses Affect Your Investment Portfolio
resources.description: An SEC bulletin showing with numbers how small yearly fee differences shrink a portfolio over 20 years.
keyPoints: Fees reduce the money left in the portfolio to earn returns
$100,000 at 4% for 20 years: ≈$208,000 with 0.25% fees
Same with 0.50% fees ≈ $198,000; with 1% fees ≈ $179,000
Compare fees before investing

stages.title: Insurance: Life & Health
stages.description: How insurance transfers risk, the difference between term life and endowment plans, and key health insurance terms such as premium, deductible, co-payment, cashless claims and portability.
learningObjectives: Explain why life insurance exists and who needs it
Distinguish term insurance from endowment plans
Define premium, deductible, co-payment and sum insured in health insurance
Explain cashless vs reimbursement claims and health insurance portability in India

explainBack.question: Explain to a young earner with dependent parents the difference between a term life plan and an endowment plan, and explain the key health insurance terms premium, deductible, co-payment and sum insured, plus how cashless claims and portability work in India.
rubric: Life insurance replaces lost income for dependents; term insurance is pure protection with no savings component, pays only if the insured dies within the term, and has the lowest premiums
An endowment plan combines insurance with savings and pays on death or survival to maturity, so it is more expensive than a term plan for the same cover

Premium is what you pay for the policy; a deductible is what you pay yourself before the insurer pays; a co-payment is a share of each claim you bear; claims reduce the sum insured available for the rest of the policy year
Cashless: the insurer pays a network hospital directly; reimbursement: you pay first and claim later (non-network hospitals are not cashless)
IRDAI portability lets you switch health insurers at renewal while keeping credit for waiting periods already served; apply at least 45 days before renewal

resources.title: Are you mixing Insurance with Investments? | Endowment Plan vs Term Insurance | What is better?
resources.description: Zerodha Varsity compares term insurance with endowment plans and the idea of keeping insurance separate from investing.
keyPoints: Compares term insurance and endowment plans
Discusses mixing insurance with investment
Explains cost differences for similar cover

resources.title: Why Buy Life Insurance
resources.description: NCFE explains why life insurance is needed and compares term, endowment, ULIP and money-back plans.
keyPoints: Life insurance supports dependents if the earner dies
Term insurance: most basic, lowest premium, no savings component
Term pays only on death within the policy term
Endowment pays on death or survival and is more expensive than term

resources.title: Health insurance primer
resources.description: Khan Academy's primer on how health insurance works, including premiums and deductibles.
keyPoints: Explains how health insurance pools risk
Introduces premiums and deductibles
Shows who pays what when you make a claim

resources.title: Glossary (Get Covered New Jersey)
resources.provider: State of New Jersey Department of Banking and Insurance
resources.description: A state insurance regulator's glossary defining premium, deductible, copayment, coinsurance and out-of-pocket maximum.
keyPoints: Premium: what you pay for the insurance itself
Deductible: what you pay before the plan starts paying
Copayment: a fixed amount per covered service
Coinsurance: a percentage of costs you pay after the deductible

resources.title: You and Your Health Insurance Policy: FAQs
resources.provider: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI)
resources.description: IRDAI's policyholder FAQ on premiums, cashless vs reimbursement claims, waiting periods, claims and co-payment.
keyPoints: Premiums generally rise with age
Cashless: insurer pays network hospitals directly; costs above limits are yours
A claim reduces the remaining sum insured (₹2 lakh claim on ₹5 lakh leaves ₹3 lakh)
Arogya Sanjeevani standard policy has a 5% co-payment

resources.title: Portability of Health Insurance
resources.provider: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI)
resources.description: IRDAI's explanation of switching health insurers without losing credit for waiting periods.
keyPoints: You can move to another insurer or plan without losing waiting-period credit
Porting is allowed only at renewal
Apply at least 45 days before the renewal date
Keep cover continuous; a grace period applies during porting

stages.title: Taxes & Retirement Savings
stages.description: How India's old and new income tax regimes differ at a general level, how tax-saving instruments such as PPF fit in, how NPS works, and why retirement planning should start early.
learningObjectives: Explain that the new tax regime is the default and what giving up deductions means
Describe the main features of PPF as a long-term, tax-advantaged savings scheme
Describe NPS Tier I and Tier II accounts
Explain why starting retirement saving early matters

explainBack.question: A 23-year-old salaried employee asks how to think about taxes and retirement. Explain how the old and new tax regimes differ in general, what PPF and NPS are, and why starting retirement savings early makes such a difference. (General education only, not tax advice.)
rubric: The new tax regime is the default for individuals; those who want the old regime must opt out. Salaried people without business income can choose each year when filing their return
The new regime does not allow most Chapter VI-A deductions such as 80C and 80D (and excludes HRA exemption), so tax-saving instruments matter mainly under the old regime
PPF: ₹500 minimum to ₹1.5 lakh maximum deposit per financial year, 15-year term extendable in 5-year blocks; deposits qualify under Section 80C and interest is tax-free
NPS Tier I is the retirement account with restricted withdrawals and tax benefits; Tier II is an optional, freely withdrawable account without tax benefits that needs an active Tier I
Starting early gives compounding more years to work; a longer horizon can absorb market ups and downs

resources.title: Why plan for retirement | Investments and retirement | Financial Literacy | Khan Academy
resources.description: Khan Academy on why retirement needs planning well in advance.
keyPoints: Why retirement needs long-term planning
The role of time and compounding
Why starting early helps

resources.title: Taxes intro | Taxes and tax forms | Financial Literacy | Khan Academy
resources.description: A Khan Academy introduction to what income taxes are and how they are applied to earnings.
keyPoints: What income tax is and why it exists
How taxable income relates to gross pay
General idea of tax brackets

resources.title: FAQs on New Tax vs Old Tax Regime
resources.provider: Income Tax Department, Government of India
resources.description: The tax department's FAQ on which regime is the default, who can switch and which deductions the new regime disallows.
keyPoints: New regime is the default from AY 2024-25; you must opt out to use the old one
Salaried taxpayers without business income can choose each year in the ITR
Business/professional earners face stricter switching rules (Form 10-IEA)
New regime disallows most deductions such as 80C, 80D and HRA exemption

resources.title: Public Provident Fund Account
resources.description: Official summary of PPF rules: deposit limits, term, loans, withdrawals and tax treatment.
keyPoints: Deposit ₹500 minimum to ₹1,50,000 maximum per financial year
Matures after 15 full financial years; extendable in 5-year blocks
Loans from year 3; withdrawals from year 7
Deposits qualify under Section 80C; interest is tax-free

resources.title: NPS - All Citizen Model
resources.provider: Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA)
resources.description: PFRDA's overview of NPS for citizens: eligibility, Tier I and Tier II accounts, investment choices and exit rules.
keyPoints: Open to Indian citizens, NRIs and OCIs aged 18–70
Tier I: retirement account, restricted withdrawals, tax benefits
Tier II: optional, withdraw anytime, no tax benefits, needs Tier I
Choose Active (own mix) or Auto (age-based life-cycle) investment choice

resources.title: Importance of Investing Early
resources.provider: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
resources.description: SEBI's investor page on why to start investing with your first income, using a compounding example.
keyPoints: Start investing from your first income
₹1,000 compounding over 40 years grows to ≈₹31,409 vs ₹4,600 with simple interest
A longer horizon helps absorb market fluctuations
Early investing supports retirement security

stages.title: Protecting Yourself & Long-Term Planning
stages.description: How to spot and avoid UPI, phishing and investment scams, why nominations matter, and how to keep long-term plans on track with asset allocation and rebalancing.
learningObjectives: Apply UPI safety rules and know where to report digital fraud in India
Identify red flags of investment scams and Ponzi-style schemes
Explain why nominations on investments matter
Explain asset allocation and when and how to rebalance a portfolio

explainBack.question: Explain to a family member how to stay safe on UPI and from 'guaranteed return' investment offers, why they should add nominees to their investments, and how a long-term investor keeps their asset mix on track over the years.
rubric: The UPI PIN is entered only to send/deduct money and is never needed to receive money; scan QR codes only to pay; never share PIN/OTP or install screen-sharing apps at a stranger's request
Report digital financial fraud quickly, e.g. on the national helpline 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in
Investment scam red flags: guaranteed/assured returns, unrealistically high returns, unregistered entities, unsolicited offers and pressure to act now; verify registration with SEBI before investing
Nomination names who can claim demat holdings or mutual fund units after the investor's death, making the claim process simpler for family; investors must either nominate or formally opt out

Asset allocation divides money among asset classes based on time horizon and risk tolerance; rebalancing restores the target mix periodically (e.g. every 6–12 months) or when it drifts beyond a set threshold

resources.title: Real world: Scams and Fraud | Teacher resources | Financial Literacy | Khan Academy
resources.description: Khan Academy's look at common real-world scams and how fraud happens.
keyPoints: Common types of scams and fraud
How scammers gain trust and create urgency
Habits that reduce the risk of being defrauded

Verify registration on SEBI's website before investing

keyPoints: Asset allocation divides a portfolio among stocks, bonds and cash

name: Personal Finance
description: Money basics with an Indian focus, from budgeting and emergency funds to credit, compounding, investing, insurance, taxes, retirement and fraud safety. Educational, not financial advice.
